approachQuestion.prompt:
Reserve Pool
There are n occupied slots, IDs 0 through n−1, each with an integer value. A command replaceLow(x) returns the current minimum (value,ID) and replaces that same slot’s value by x. replaceHigh(x) analogously returns the maximum by value, ties by smaller ID, then replaces its value by x. Example: initial=[4,1,7], commands=[replaceLow(9),replaceHigh(2),replaceHigh(0)] → [(1,1),(9,1),(7,2)].

2 ≤ n ≤ 100000; n ≤ q ≤ 200000 online commands. Values fit signed 32 bits. Initial input is read-only; slot count stays n. Answers must be emitted before the next command arrives. Which approach best meets this contract?
constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100000; n ≤ q ≤ 200000 online commands. Values fit signed 32 bits. Initial input is read-only; slot count stays n. Answers must be emitted before the next command arrives.

options.text: Maintain a min-heap ordered by (value,ID) and a max-heap ordered by value descending then ID ascending. Both hold all slot IDs, with ID-to-position arrays and a shared current-value array. Choose the requested root, report its old pair, replace the shared value, and repair that ID’s entry in both heaps, updating positions after swaps.
options.feedback: The selected slot changes in both orderings. Position arrays locate it in each heap, allowing both invariants to be repaired without searching or retaining obsolete copies.

options.text: Keep slots in a value-ordered array; remove the requested endpoint and insert its replacement at the correct sorted position by shifting.
options.feedback: The ordering and tie rule are correct, but repeated shifts are avoidable.

options.text: Maintain both heaps but repair only the heap from which the root was selected.
options.feedback: With initial [1,2], replaceLow(9) must make ID 0 the maximum; the unrepaired max-heap can still report ID 1.

options.text: Use one min-heap; for replaceHigh read its final array element as the maximum.
options.feedback: The last leaf is not necessarily largest. A valid min-heap [1,9,2] has maximum 9 at the other leaf.

Both heaps must reference the same slot value and have updated position maps. Repair that ID in both heaps after replacement; changing only the heap used for the current command leaves the opposite query stale.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze A with bottom-up construction of two binary heaps and dense position/value arrays. Let n be slots and q≥n online commands. Repairs in each heap are iterative and positions use direct indexing, with no hash tables, stale entries or command history. Choose the tightest time and auxiliary-space pair.
constraints: Use the tightest worst-case bound for the whole input unless amortized or expected accounting is explicitly specified. Comparing or moving a record and arithmetic on machine words take constant time.

Exclude supplied input and returned output from auxiliary space. Count working arrays, queues, tables and call stacks. Output storage is separate and is not used as workspace. Heap repairs and traversals are iterative. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n + q log(n+1)) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + q log(n+1)) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: A constant number of n-sized arrays supports two logarithmic repairs per command.
details: Build both heaps and arrays in O(n). Each command reads one root and repairs a known slot along at most one path in each heap, costing O(log(n+1)); adverse replacements attain that cost. A constant number of n-sized arrays uses O(n) storage. No snapshot grows with q; emitted old pairs are output only.
“O(n+q) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: Changing a value can move it across a heap’s full height.
“O(n + q log(n+1)) time, O(n+q) auxiliary space”: This overcounts retained history: each slot has one entry per heap and no old entries remain.
“O(nq) time, O(1) auxiliary space”: Both heaps and locator arrays occupy space; the method avoids scanning all slots.
